intro: Three students sit down for lunch in Pilsen. One is from Buenos Aires, one from Madrid, one from Mexico City. They order the same juice with two different words, say gracias with two different sounds, and use three different pronouns for you. Nobody misunderstands anyone. That table is the Spanish-speaking world in miniature: twenty countries and Puerto Rico, hundreds of millions of speakers, one language with many voices. This unit is a map of that world and a guide to moving through it.

In the first chapter you will learn where Spanish is official, how it came to the United States and to Illinois, and how it varies: vos in Argentina and Central America, vosotros in Spain, the th sound of Madrid and the s of everywhere else, guagua and camión and colectivo for one bus. You will trace words back to Arabic (almohada, ojalá), Nahuatl (chocolate, tomate) and Taíno (huracán, canoa), and see that Spanish has always borrowed.

In the second chapter you will learn register: when to say tú and when to say usted, how to open and close a formal letter, how to soften a request with podría and quisiera, which words are false friends, and how to read the signs, menus and headlines you pass every day. By the end you will be able to write to a company for a summer job in Spanish that sounds serious, text your cousin in Spanish that sounds like you, and know the difference on purpose.
bigQuestion: How does one language serve twenty countries and every situation from a text to a job letter, and how do you choose the right Spanish for the person in front of you?

timeline.t: Arabic-speaking armies enter the Iberian Peninsula; centuries of contact give Spanish words like azúcar, aceite and ojalá
Granada falls, Nebrija publishes the first grammar of Castilian, and Columbus reaches the Caribbean, where Spanish meets Taíno
Spanish speakers reach Mexico and begin borrowing Nahuatl words: chocolate, tomate, aguacate
St. Augustine is founded in Florida, the oldest continuously occupied European settlement in the present-day United States
The Real Academia Española is founded in Madrid to care for the language
The Grito de Dolores on September 16 begins Mexico's war of independence; most of Spanish America follows over the next decade
The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo moves the border; Spanish speakers in the Southwest become residents of the United States
Puerto Rico passes from Spain to the United States; Puerto Ricans become U.S. citizens in 1917
Equatorial Guinea gains independence from Spain and keeps Spanish as an official language
The U.S. census counts more than 62 million Hispanic or Latino residents, more than 2 million of them in Illinois
Spanish is official in 20 countries and Puerto Rico and is heard daily in Pilsen, Little Village and Humboldt Park

words.d: Spanish-speaking, or a Spanish speaker — el mundo hispanohablante spans twenty countries and Puerto Rico
you (informal singular) in Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay and much of Central America: vos hablás, vos sos
you all (informal) in Spain: vosotros habláis, sois; Latin America uses ustedes
pronouncing z and soft c as s, the norm in Latin America; most of Spain uses the th sound (la distinción)
a regional word — guagua, camión, colectivo and autobús are all one bus
the language of the Aztecs, still spoken in Mexico; source of chocolate, tomate, aguacate, chile
register — the level of formality set by pronoun, verb endings, greetings and word choice
you (formal) — takes the él/ella verb forms; for elders, teachers, employers and strangers
Dear (formal) — opens a formal letter with a title and a colon: Estimada señora Herrera:
Sincerely — the standard closing of a formal letter
could you — the conditional of poder, the softener of polite requests: ¿Podría ayudarme?
a false friend — a word that looks English but means something else: embarazada, éxito, carpeta

test.q: Spanish is an official language in how many countries?
test.why: Twenty countries have Spanish as an official language, on three continents, plus Puerto Rico, a U.S. territory.

test.q: Which sentence would you expect from a speaker in Buenos Aires?
test.why: Argentina uses vos, and the vos form of ser is sos. Usted eres mixes usted with a tú verb and is wrong everywhere.

test.q: The vosotros form of vivir is
test.why: Vivís is the vosotros present form (and also the vos form). Viven is ustedes, vivimos nosotros, vivid the command.

test.q: A speaker from Mexico City pronounces the z in zapato
test.why: Latin America uses the seseo: z and soft c sound like s. Most of Spain uses the th sound.

test.q: Which word for bus would you hear in Puerto Rico?
test.why: Guagua is the Caribbean word for bus. Colectivo is Argentina, micro is Chile, and ordenador is Spain's word for computer.

test.q: Which word came into Spanish from Nahuatl?
test.why: Tomate is Nahuatl, like chocolate and aguacate. Almohada is Arabic, hamaca is Taíno, papa is Quechua.

test.q: Which word came into Spanish from Taíno and then into English?
test.why: Huracán is Taíno and became hurricane in English through Spanish. Azúcar is Arabic, chile is Nahuatl, palta is Quechua.

test.q: Which Chicago neighborhood is the center of the city's Puerto Rican community?
test.why: Humboldt Park, with Paseo Boricua on Division Street, is the heart of Puerto Rican Chicago. Pilsen and Little Village are largely Mexican American.

test.q: Which sentence correctly addresses a teacher you have just met?
test.why: Usted takes the él/ella form tiene. Tienes, tenés and tenéis are all informal forms.

test.q: Which greeting opens a formal letter correctly?
test.why: Estimado agrees with a man, the title is lowercase, and the greeting ends with a colon. Querido and Hola are informal; Estimada is feminine.

test.q: Which request is the most polite?
choices: ¿Me podría traer la cuenta, por favor?
test.why: The conditional podría plus por favor is the softest form. Tráigame is a command; quiero states a want; me trae is polite but plainer.

test.q: "Estoy muy embarazada" said by a student who arrived late means
test.why: Embarazada means pregnant. A student who meant embarrassed should say avergonzada or me da mucha vergüenza.

test.q: A sign reads "Se busca cajero." It means
test.why: Se busca plus a job title is a help-wanted sign. The impersonal se has no specific subject.

test.q: After a boss says "Puedes tutearme," which sentence is correct?
test.why: Tutear means to use tú, so the verb becomes estás. Está tú mixes registers, and estáis is vosotros.

test.q: The headline "Sube el precio del pan en Chicago" tells you that
test.why: Subir means to rise. Headlines use the present tense and short verbs like subir and bajar for prices.

write.prompt: Escribe dos textos sobre el mismo trabajo de verano: una carta formal de 6 a 8 oraciones a la dueña de una empresa (Estimada, usted, tu experiencia, tu disponibilidad, Atentamente) y un mensaje informal de 3 a 4 oraciones a un primo (tú, ¿qué tal?, un abrazo). Write a formal job letter and an informal message about the same job; make the register of each clear.
tips: In the letter, use usted forms only: tiene, puede, su; in the message, use tú forms only: tienes, puedes, tu.
Open the letter with Estimado or Estimada plus a title and a colon, and close with Atentamente and your full name.
Soften requests with podría, quisiera or ¿sería posible…?, and check for false friends like embarazada, éxito and carpeta.
Use the regional word your family uses (carro or coche, jugo or zumo), but no texting abbreviations in the letter.
Read both texts aloud; if a line from the letter sounds like a text to a friend, rewrite it.
